The Surprising Connection Between Grief and Gratitude

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1661 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Life as I knew it quietly began to unravel on a drizzly January morning in 2022.
  • Recent findings suggest that I was standing at the kitchen sink in a puffer jacket, staring out at my favorite persimmon tree, now bare.
  • Now that the kids were gone, my husband Mark and I conserved energy by leaving the downstairs heat off, telling each other we couldn’t justify heating the whole house just to keep the kitchen warm.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Life as I knew it quietly began to unravel on a drizzly January morning in 2022.

Recent findings suggest that I was standing at the kitchen sink in a puffer jacket, staring out at my favorite persimmon tree, now bare. Only weeks before, the tree had been so full of persimmons that we collected them in huge plastic garbage cans for our neighbors to take by the grocery bagful. Our Labrador-ish mutt, Buster, was fat from persimmon overconsumption.

Now that the kids were gone, my husband Mark and I conserved energy by leaving the downstairs heat off, telling each other we couldn’t justify heating the whole house just to keep the kitchen warm. We were real empty-nesters, ready to downsize.

Recent findings suggest that within weeks, we stripped our house of everything personal. We took down family photos, scraped butterfly stickers from hidden corners, and painted over the teal walls preteen girls had decorated. All traces of our family life vanished. We put our home on the market. It was the end of an era.

Sources indicate that in December, my seemingly super-fit mom was diagnosed with ovarian cancer. Our house still hadn’t sold—by the time we put it on the market, mortgage rates had started climbing for the first time in two decades—but I moved into my childhood bedroom at my parents’ home to help my dad care for my mom. She passed away four months later.

According to recent reports, A week before my mom’s memorial, I myself was diagnosed with invasive breast cancer. And a few days after my first cancer-related surgery, a close cousin died of an accidental overdose just after his 50th birthday.

In a recent development, also during that time, a dear college friend, a fit, athletic doctor, had a fatal heart attack. And while I was having radiation for my breast cancer, our beloved dog Buster was diagnosed with lymphoma and needed to be put down.

Sources indicate that other losses were expected and even positive. Our house finally sold, and so we remarked goodbye to the home where we had raised our four kids. I packed up that house through tears—for my mom, for my health, for my beloved dog and cousin and college friend, sobbing as I threw away things that marked my kids’ childhoods: boxes of ribbons from horse indicates and swim meets, SAT score reports, so many old shoes and backpacks, homemade Harry Potter wands.

Recent findings suggest that mark and I put our stuff in storage and moved in with my dad for real while we renovated a new house in Berkeley. I loved this time with my dad; it made my cancer treatment and everything else bearable. He had always been my person, and now I got to cry and laugh with him every day, with no space between us.

About a year after my mom died, we finally moved into our new house. The first morning I woke up there and looked out the window at the whole Bay Area, I was astonished to see not one, but four rainbows touching down on the water of the San Francisco Bay. I felt welcomed and reassured that I was right where I was meant to be.

Sources indicate that but then my brother-in-law Brian was diagnosed with a malignant brain tumor, the kind that doesn’t usually respond to chemo or radiation. They did everything anyway—brain surgery, chemotherapy, radiation, experimental drugs, an electromagnetic cap, expensive immunotherapy from Germany—but less than nine months later, he too passed away. I’ve never known a man with a bigger heart than Brian; when he died, we lost the emotional center on Mark’s side of the family.

Our family was devastated. Again.

Sources indicate that with each of these losses and life changes, I picked myself up and told my friends that at least it wasn’t my dad. When my dad dies, I’m going to stay in bed for a year, I said. When my dad dies, expect my complete collapse. I started believing that I could bear anything except for losing my father, my oldest and dearest friend. The loss of my father would leave a hole in my heart I knew I could never fill.

And then, in April of 2025, one month to the day after we lost Brian, my 84-year-old dad passed away.

He was still driving, doing Pilates, and walking his dog Annie around his hilly neighborhood. He was still sharp as a tack, still hilarious, still going out every day to meet his many friends or his brother, Jud. He still volunteered and mentored others.

One week, he was fully with us, bringing me a burrito for dinner at my nephew’s Little League game, taking us to dinner at the club where he’d been a lifelong member, buying tickets to a Giants game. The next week, he was gone.

Recent findings suggest that my brother and I decided it “made sense” to sell our childhood home, a place that had anchored our extended family for nearly 50 years. But I could not make sense of how I could lose everything that centered me, my whole foundation, so fucking fast.

Still, I didn’t utterly collapse. I learned how to grieve in small moments throughout the day; how to keep putting one foot in front of the other while still feeling loss. I cried before and after work as I walked my dad’s sweet little Annie. I broke down at the grocery store, in restaurants, while hiking with friends, at the post office. I wept while packing up my parents’ house and while pulling apart their photo albums. I was exhausted, hollowed out.

My heart was broken, but I got out of bed every morning.

I started latest, truly energizing work projects and slogged through my parents’ stuff and another year of difficult firsts. The first Father’s Day without my dad, the first family birthday not celebrated at my parents’ house. As the first Thanksgiving without my dad and Brian approached, my therapist remarked that grief was often surprisingly life-enhancing. That was turning out to be true for me.

Thanksgiving has always been my favorite holiday. I usually host our big family, and I always have a lot to say at dinnertime about what I am grateful for. That year, the intimate connection between loss and gratitude had become painfully obvious to me.

In a recent development, genuine gratitude—when we really pause to acknowledge how valuable something is—inherently involves recognizing the impermanence of that thing. True gratitude carries the awareness that what we’re grateful for won’t last forever; it’s here now but could be gone tomorrow. That awareness is what makes a moment feel more vivid and precious.

Sources indicate that I think one gift of loss is that it can make us more intensely grateful. Not because we’re anxious about losing someone or something, but because we’ve learned viscerally that everything is temporary—and therefore extraordinary.

In a recent development, this crucible of loss and gratitude burned away my tolerance for anything that didn’t feel essential, helping me return to a deep spirituality. Standing at the edge of my own mortality and watching the structures of my life dissolve one by one fundamentally reordered my sense of what matters. Grief is the price of love, and it teaches us that love is what matters most.

Sources indicate that so much loss has made pretense impossible for me. Grief strips us down and cracks us open, breaking down the defenses and distractions that keep us living on the surface. In the past few years, I’ve been to deep places, emotionally and existentially, that only truth can reach. I can’t un-know that now. Superficiality has started to feel like I’m being asked to forget the hard-won truth about how fragile and precious life actually is.

When we’re grieving, we can’t pretend. We can’t avoid our own vulnerability or the fact that everything ends. And while that’s devastating, it’s also strangely liberating. I feel more at peace, more permeable, more present, more profoundly loving, more alive to the texture of my lived experience. I’m attuned to what’s real and meaningful. I feel closer to and more in love with my friends and family than ever before. I feel things so deeply, and that depth is a kind of richness.

It has been revealed that all of this is to say that growth happens in the broken-open places in our hearts. Loss and gratitude both dissolve the boundary between ourselves and the larger human experience. When we love and when we grieve, we join an ancient river of sorrow and love that connects us to everyone who has ever loved and lost.

Industry observers note that I would never choose the losses I’ve endured. I’d give anything to have my people back, and not to have had cancer. But this is the grief-gratitude paradox: I also wouldn’t trade what grief has taught me, how deeply I feel, or who I am now because of all I’ve lost.

Recent findings suggest that so this Thanksgiving, I’ll be at the table again, with fewer people than I’d like but more love than I ever knew I had room for. When it’s my turn to say what I’m grateful for, I won’t need to think about it. Every single moment is a gift. It’s all temporary, and it’s all extraordinary.

Industry observers note that christine Carter, Ph.D. is a Senior Fellow at the Greater Good Science Center. She is the author of The New Adolescence: Raising Happy and Successful Teens in an Age of Anxiety and Distraction (BenBella, 2020), The Sweet Spot: How to Accomplish More by Doing Less (Ballantine Books, 2015), and Raising Happiness: 10 Simple Steps for More Joyful Kids and Happier Parents (Random House, 2010). A former director of the GGSC, she served for many years as author of its parenting blog, Raising Happiness. Find out more about Christine here.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Though seemingly worlds apart today, Ciudad Juárez and El Paso were one city until the Rio Grande river was established as the border between Mexico and the US in 1848.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that can the “open wound” of the Mexico-US border be healed? Sutura, a newly introduced bi-national art programme in Ciudad Juárez, Chihuahua, and El Paso, Texas (18 November-22 November), looks beyond stereotypes of violence surrounding the Mexico-US border and explores how art might help mend the region’s many wounds, even imperfectly or temporarily. Sutura (Spanish for “suture”) brings together more than 100 artists across 20 venues, including the El Paso Museum of Art (EPMA), the Stanlee and Gerald Rubin Center for the Visual Arts and the Museo de Arte de Ciudad Juárez (MACJ), alongside independent projects and pop-up exhibitions.

Recent findings suggest that juárez has long been associated with sensational narratives of violence. Persistent migration issues, heightened by stricter border controls and alarming deportation measures, feminicides, the drug war and hyper-surveillance have shaped the local context. These aspects have permeated cultural production. “Endless works have explored this territory as a symbol and symptom of an apocalyptic future,” writes Willivaldo Delgadillo in his book-length essay Fabular Juárez (2020).

Though seemingly worlds apart today, Ciudad Juárez and El Paso were one city until the Rio Grande river was established as the border between Mexico and the US in 1848. Despite tensions between their respective countries, the two cities are still connected by education, jobs and transit.

Industry observers note that “On each side of the border, nuanced and contrasting fears and ideologies coexist, but there is also community,” Edgar Picazo Merino, Sutura’s founder and lead organiser, tells The Art Newspaper. “For all of us who live here, the border is a personal, lived experience.” Picazo founded the independent initiative Azul Arena in 2019 to support the Juárez-El Paso art scene; it established a permanent space in Juárez in 2022.

In a recent development, central to thinking about the border in the context of Sutura and more broadly is Chicana writer Gloria Anzaldúa’s 1987 metaphor of the border as an “open wound”. “The Third World grates against the first and bleeds,” Anzaldúa wrote. “And before a scab forms, it haemorrhages again, the lifeblood of two worlds merging to form a third country—a border culture.” The “open wound” concept has become commonplace in border literature, Picazo says, while Sutura seeks to deconstruct it: “If the border is a wound, how can the arts suture its many wounds, while opening places of reflection and interaction?”.

Detail of Justin Favela's Mantecore (White Tiger) (2017), featured in Qué tanto es tantito, a group show on view at San Luis Contemporáneo, Ciudad Juárez Courtesy Haydee Alonso.

Recent findings suggest that sutura builds on binational initiatives like Insite, which emerged in 1992 at the San Diego-Tijuana border and initially featured site-specific installations before changing formats. It also draws on regional ties. The Juárez-El Paso Border Biennial, launched in 2008 by the EPMA and MACJ, is presently in its eighth edition, Imagining the Border (until 2 May 2027). Co-curated by the Juárez-based curators Adriana Miramontes Olivas and Alejandro Morales, it features more than 80 works by artists based within 300 miles of El Paso and Juárez.

It has been revealed that “A border that is always there, one that weighs heavily on our communities, rarely lets us imagine it,” Morales says. “This edition opens that space, offering a plural and rigorous portrait of it as living territory.”.

The Border Biennial has strived to shift perceptions. “The biennial has national relevance, moving beyond portrayals of the border as perpetually on fire, highlighting its creative richness and cultural legacies,” notes Edward Hayes Jr, the director of the EPMA, adding that the project requires overcoming diplomatic and logistical challenges. “We aim for the biennial to be a structural project for both institutions,” says Christian Diego Diego, MACJ’s director. Diego adds that over its past and current editions, the Border Biennial has featured more than 400 works by around 270 artists, “reflecting the border’s ambivalence and multiple stories”. Sutura’s programme includes visits to the biennial, reflecting dialogue with the artists, curators and venues.

Sutura also grew from asking how a Juárez-El Paso art week might unfold. Border initiatives are gaining visibility. The fair Material, through its two-year Projects programme, has supported Azul Arena and the Juárez curatorial duo Un Dique with mentorship and free participation in its Mexico City and Guadalajara fairs. Un Dique joins Sutura by curating theexhibition Border Kaijus on border hypervigilance. Two other border cities have recently created art weeks amid growing efforts to decentralise a national scene largely centred on Mexico City: Tijuana held its second art week in July; Mexicali held its first in April.

It has been revealed that “There is a growing scene among border Mexican cities with spaces and initiatives interacting,” says Andres Payan Estrada, the director and chief curator of the Stanlee and Gerald Rubin Center for the Visual Arts and Sutura’s artistic strategy director. Still, he adds, Sutura is not an art week: “It is a non-commercial collaborative initiative with a strong community component.”.

Installation view of the group show Costuras Territoriales at the Stanlee and Gerald Rubin Center for the Visual Arts at the University of Texas, El Paso Courtesy of the Stanlee and Gerald Rubin Center for the Visual Arts at the University of Texas, El Paso.

It has been revealed that in El Paso, institutional participation is strong. During Sutura, the Rubin Center is showing Costuras Territoriales (until 12 December), curated by Payan and featuring textile-inspired works by five women artists connected to the border, including Teresa Margolles, Tania Candiani and Juárez-based Olga Guerra. “The way in which artists explore the border has sometimes become a cliché,” Guerra says. “I intend to reflect relationality through a more poetic approach, incorporating locally found organic materials and fibres, along with reused materials.”.

Independent initiatives are vital in Juárez, where conventional galleries are non-existent. Picazo’s Azul Arena, a pillar of the city’s scene, will present the exhibition En la línea, exploring the line as a metaphor for the border. The Juárez-based artist Haydee Alonso, co-founder of San Luis Contemporáneo, will curate the exhibition ¿Qué tanto es tantito? there and present a performance at Azul Arena. “My work analyses transborder relations through the body and objects, opening spaces within the complexities of living here,” claims Alonso, who crosses the border daily to teach at the University of Texas at El Paso. Both projects have received support from the Mellon Foundation, which Alonso and Picazo consider crucial to local initiatives. In El Paso, where independent spaces are relatively scarce, The Falstaff, a community-centred hybrid art space, will host exhibitions and concerts.

Installation view ofthe group exhibiton Qué tanto es tantito, group show on view at San Luis Contemporáneo, Ciudad Juárez Courtesy Haydee Alonso.

Sources indicate that sutura also supports the local scene by showcasing six El Paso and Juárez projects selected through an open call, with each project receiving $3,000 for production costs. The photography exhibition Relatos de la Frontera: Cuerpo y Espacio explores border perspectives through the body and space Another show, Tierra Suelta, presents works inspired by children of migrant families that settled in Juárez for reasons other than the “American dream”, integrating a community activation into the programme. These projects foreground local perspectives in a region often depicted by outsiders, alongside established artists—primarily Mexican and Mexican American—whose work reflects on the border.

Picazo acknowledges the complexities of a bi-national event: not everyone can cross both ways because of visa restrictions and other issues. “The programme has parallel activities so you can experience Sutura even from one side of the border,” he says.

Sutura speaks more of resilience than crisis, more of possibility than scarcity.“Historically, the border is explained one-dimensionally, yet a myriad of dynamics co-exist here,” Picazo notes. “Sutura exists as a relational art encounter.”.

#183394. Tech Report: The Four Buddhist Mantras for Turning Fear into Love

Tech Report: The Four Buddhist Mantras for Turning Fear into Love

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1554 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Themarginalian

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that “Fearlessness is what love seeks,” Hannah Arendt wrote in her magnificent early work on love and how to live with fear.
  • This notion of presence as the antidote to fear and the crucible of love is as old as the human heart, as old as the consciousness that first felt the blade of anticipatory loss pressed against the exposed underbelly of the longing for connection.
  • In the general Buddhist style of befriending complexity through simplicity and with his particular gift for simple words strung into a rosary of immense wisdom radiating immense kindness, Thich Nhat Hanh writes:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that “Fearlessness is what love seeks,” Hannah Arendt wrote in her magnificent early work on love and how to live with fear. “Such fearlessness exists only in the complete calm that can no longer be shaken by events expected of the future… Hence the only valid tense is the present, the Now.”.

This notion of presence as the antidote to fear and the crucible of love is as old as the human heart, as old as the consciousness that first felt the blade of anticipatory loss pressed against the exposed underbelly of the longing for connection. It is at the center of millennia-old Buddhist philosophy and comes alive afresh, in a splendidly practical way, in Fear: Essential Wisdom for Getting Through the Storm (public library) by the great Vietnamese Buddhist teacher and peace activist Thich Nhat Hanh, who continued to enrich, ennoble, and empower with his teachings well into his nineties.

In the general Buddhist style of befriending complexity through simplicity and with his particular gift for simple words strung into a rosary of immense wisdom radiating immense kindness, Thich Nhat Hanh writes:.

We have a great, habitual fear inside ourselves. We’re afraid of many things — of our own death, of losing our loved ones, of change, of being alone. The practice of mindfulness helps us to touch nonfear. It’s only here and now that we can experience total relief, total happiness… In the practice of Buddhism, we see that all mental formations — including compassion, love, fear, sorrow, and despair — are organic in nature. We don’t need to be afraid of any of them, because transformation is always possible.

In a recent development, such transformation is possible only through deliberate practice — none more challenging, or more rewarding, than the practice of transforming fear into love. In consonance with his teaching that “to love without knowing how to love wounds the person we love,” he anchors this transmutation practice in four mantras “effective for watering the seeds of happiness in yourself and your beloved and for transforming fear, suffering, and loneliness.”.

Industry observers note that unlike a prayer — which channels a hope at some imagined entity capable of interceding in favor of that hope and has only as a side benefit (though arguably its only real and robust benefit) the psychological self-clarification that comes from honing our hopes in language — a mantra is not addressed at anything or anyone external and is entirely devoted to distilling the object of hope to its clearest essence. This, in and of itself, transforms the hope into an intent, making it more actionable — but also saving it from the particular complacency against which Descartes admonished as he considered the vital relationship between fear and hope. A mantra is therefore not a form of magical thinking, for while there is a sense of magic to how such distillation seems to shift the situation by its very utterance, it is an entirely practical sort of magic, for a mantra simply clarifies, concentrates, and consecrates intent, and all meaningful transformation springs from purposeful, devoted intent.

According to recent reports, A mantra is a kind of magic formula that, once uttered, can entirely change a situation. It can change us, and it can change others. But this magic formula must be spoken in concentration, with body and mind focused as one. What you say in this state of being becomes a mantra.

Within this conceptual framework, he offers four mantras for transforming fear into love, beginning with “Mantra for Offering Your Presence.” A generation after Simone Weil insisted that “attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity,” he writes:.

It has been revealed that the most precious gift you can give to the one you love is your true presence. So the first mantra is very simple: “Dear one, I am here for you.”.

Simple though this mantra might seem, he reminds us that actually cultivating the capacity for it — the capacity for presence, which is where our capacity for love resides — is intensely difficult against the tidal wave of demand and distraction that sweeps everyday life and sweeps us along with it, leaving us always on the brink of drowning, bereft of what Emerson celebrated as “the power to swell the moment from the resources of our own heart until it supersedes sun & moon & solar system in its expanding immensity.”.

A century after Tolstoy insisted that “love is a present activity only,” Thich Nhat Hanh gently reminds us that the greatest resource of our own heart — our greatest source of power, our mightiest antidote to fear — is the quality of love we give through the quality of our presence:.

According to recent reports, when you love someone, the best thing you can offer that person is your presence. How can you love if you are not there? Come back to yourself, look into [their] eyes, and say, “Darling, you know something? I’m here for you.” You’re offering [them] your presence. You’re not preoccupied with the past or the future; you are there for your beloved. You must say this with your body and with your mind at the same time, and then you will see the transformation.

Such crystalline presence is the prerequisite for the next mantra — “Mantra for Recognizing Your Beloved”:.

The second mantra is, “Darling, I know you are there, and I am so happy.”.

According to recent reports, to be there is the first step, and recognizing the presence of the other person is the second step. Because you are fully there, you recognize that the presence of your beloved is something very precious. You embrace your beloved with mindfulness, and he or she will bloom like a flower. To be loved means first of all to be recognized as existing.

In a sentiment of especial relevance and consolation in these disembodied times, he reminds us that these mantras can be performed across distance, across wires and cables and screens, not requiring the physical presence of the beloved — however they are articulated, they are at bottom meditations containing all four elements of true love as described by the Buddha: love, compassion, joy, and freedom.

While the third mantra, “Mantra for Relieving Suffering,” could be magnified and deepened by the atomic rewards of Thich Nhat Hanh’s “hugging meditation,” it too can be extended across the digital distance:.

Even before you do anything to help, your wholehearted presence already brings some relief, because when we suffer, we have great need for presence of the person we love. If we are suffering and the person we love ignores us, we suffer more. So what you can do — right away — is to manifest your true presence to your beloved and say the mantra with all your mindfulness: “Dear one, I know you are suffering. That is why I am here for you.” And already your loved one will feel better.

Your presence is a miracle, your understanding of his or her pain is a miracle, and you are able to offer this aspect of your love immediately. Really try to be there, for yourself, for life, for the people you love. Recognize the presence of those who live in the same place as you, and try to be there when one of them is suffering, because your presence is so precious for this person.

The fourth and final mantra, “Mantra for Reaching Out to Ask for Help,” seems on the surface to be self-concerned, but is in fact the crucible of self-care from which all unselfish love and presence spring. It is also, Thich Nhat Hanh observes, the most difficult of the four, for it dwells in the place of our greatest vulnerability and at the same time pushes us to lean on our most crippling crutch:.

It has been revealed that this mantra is for when you are suffering and you believe that your beloved has caused you suffering. If someone else had done the same wrong to you, you would have suffered less. But this is the person you love the most, so you suffer deeply, and the last thing you feel like doing is to ask that person for help… So now it is your pride that is the obstacle to reconciliation and healing. According to the teaching of the Buddha, in true love there is no place for pride.

In a recent development, when you are suffering like this, you must go to the person you love and ask for his or her help. That is true love. Do not let pride keep you apart. You must overcome your pride. You must always go to him or her. That is what this mantra is for. Practice for yourself first, to bring about oneness of your body and mind before going to the other person to say the fourth mantra: “Dear one, I am suffering; please help.” This is very simple but very hard to do.

Complement this particular fragment of the wholly soul-salving Fear: Essential Wisdom for Getting Through the Storm with Seneca on overcoming fear and Audre Lorde on turning fear into fire, then revisit the great Buddhist teacher Pema Chödrön on transformation through difficult times.

#183393. Most Teens Care, So Why Don’t They Always Help?

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1492 w)

Most Teens Care, So Why Don’t They Always Help?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1492 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A student notices a classmate eating lunch alone.
  • Most adults assume the challenge is getting young people to care.
  • We often imagine compassion as a straightforward process: Notice suffering, feel concern, take action.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A student notices a classmate eating lunch alone. Another sees a peer being excluded from a group chat. Someone knows a friend has been struggling but hesitates before reaching out. Why?

Most adults assume the challenge is getting young people to care. But after spending years studying adolescent compassion, I have come to believe that caring may not be the central problem.

The question is what happens next.

We often imagine compassion as a straightforward process: Notice suffering, feel concern, take action. Yet anyone who has worked with adolescents knows that the path is rarely so simple. Young people are navigating friendships, social hierarchies, identity development, and concerns about belonging, all while learning how to manage their own emotions. In these moments, compassion is not simply a feeling. It is a decision unfolding within a complex social world.

In our recent research developing the Youth Compassion Measure, an assessment of compassionate responding, we find that most adolescents recognize when a peer is struggling. What varies is whether that recognition translates into helping. Across hundreds of students, four factors consistently shape whether compassion becomes action: peer dynamics, social risk, emotional regulation, and intrinsic motivation.

Understanding these factors may help parents, educators, and youth-serving professionals better support compassionate action in young people.

One of the clearest findings from our work is that adolescents were more likely to help when the person experiencing distress was someone they knew well.

At first glance, this may seem obvious. Most of us are more likely to check on a close friend than a stranger. Yet this finding points to a deeper truth about adolescence: compassion unfolds within relationships.

It has been revealed that during adolescence, friendships become central to daily life. Young people are figuring out who they are, where they belong, and how they fit into their social worlds. Relationships provide security, identity, and connection. Unsurprisingly, those same relationships shape compassionate responding.

This means that compassion is not simply an individual trait. It is also social.

In a recent development, when educators talk about creating compassionate schools, they often focus on teaching empathy or kindness. Those efforts matter. But our findings suggest that fostering strong, supportive relationships may be just as important. Young people appear more willing to take compassionate action when they feel connected to the people around them.

In a recent development, in other words, belonging may do more than improve well-being. It may help create the conditions that allow compassion to flourish.

If relationships explain who adolescents help, social risk helps explain why they sometimes do not.

Consider a common scenario. A student witnesses a peer being teased. They know the behavior is hurtful. They may even want to intervene. Yet stepping forward could carry consequences. They may worry about being judged, excluded, or embarrassed, or becoming a target themselves.

Our findings suggest that adolescents are often weighing these possibilities, consciously or unconsciously, before deciding how to respond.

This is one reason public conversations about bullying can be so frustrating. When videos circulate online, attention swiftly turns to the bystanders. Why didn’t anyone help?

Industry observers note that the question assumes that recognizing suffering naturally leads to action. But social reality is more complicated.

Young people are often assessing multiple things at once: the seriousness of the situation, who is involved, who is watching, what might happen if they intervene, and what might happen if they do not. What appears from the outside as indifference may actually be a moment of conflict between compassion and self-protection.

Recent findings suggest that this perspective does not excuse harmful behavior or passivity. But it does encourage us to understand helping as a social act rather than a purely moral one.

If we want young people to act compassionately, we need environments where compassionate action is socially supported instead of socially costly.

Perhaps the most surprising finding from our study is that recognizing suffering alone did not consistently predict helping.

Many students understood that someone was struggling. The difference was what happened after that recognition occurred.

One of the strongest predictors of compassionate action is distress tolerance, the ability to remain engaged in the presence of emotional discomfort. This matters because witnessing another person’s suffering is often uncomfortable. We may feel sadness, anxiety, uncertainty, helplessness, or fear of saying the wrong thing. Adolescents experience these emotions, too.

In a recent development, imagine a teenager whose friend is crying. The challenge is not simply recognizing that the friend is upset, it’s navigating the delicate space between over-identifying with another person’s suffering and distancing oneself from it. Too much emotional absorption can lead to overwhelm and withdrawal. Too much distance can lead to disengagement. Compassion requires something different: remaining connected to another person’s experience while maintaining enough emotional balance to respond effectively.

People sometimes assume that compassion and empathy are the same thing. They are not. Empathy allows us to resonate with another person’s experience. Compassion involves channeling that awareness into a desire to alleviate suffering. Doing so requires emotional regulation. Without it, concern can become overwhelm, uncertainty, or avoidance. Instead of moving toward suffering, we move away from it.

Our findings suggest that compassionate action depends not only on recognizing another person’s distress, but also on the ability to stay present with that distress without becoming consumed by it. In this sense, emotional regulation is not separate from compassion; it helps make compassion possible.

Industry observers note that for parents and educators, this finding has crucial practical implications. Teaching young people how to navigate difficult emotions may strengthen their capacity for compassionate action. Skills such as mindfulness, emotional awareness, reflection, and distress tolerance are not simply tools for managing stress. They may also be the very capacities that help adolescents transform caring into action by staying engaged when helping feels uncertain, vulnerable, or emotionally difficult.

Even when adolescents care and have the emotional skills to stay engaged, one additional factor matters: motivation.

Recent findings suggest that in our study, intrinsic prosocial motivation was one of the strongest predictors of helping. Simply put, adolescents who genuinely wanted to help others were more likely to translate concern into action.

This may sound self-evident, but it carries key implications.

Adults often try to encourage helping through external incentives, praise, rewards, or behavioral expectations. While these approaches can influence behavior, our findings suggest that compassionate action is especially powerful when it emerges from internal values and genuine concern for others.

Industry observers note that young people are constantly asking themselves what kind of person they want to be. When helping becomes connected to identity, meaning, and purpose, compassionate action appears more likely to follow.

This suggests that fostering compassion is about more than encouraging kind behavior. It is also about helping young people develop a sense of responsibility toward others and a meaningful connection to shared humanity.

Taken together, these findings challenge a common assumption.

Recent findings suggest that there is a tendency to treat moments of inaction as moments of moral failure. We see a young person remain silent, fail to intervene, or walk past another person’s suffering, and we assume we understand what happened.

Yet our research suggests that these moments are often more complicated than they appear.

They unfold within social worlds shaped by belonging, friendship, identity, uncertainty, vulnerability, and the deeply human desire to remain connected to others. They are influenced by relationships, social risks, emotional capacities, and personal motivations.

What looks like indifference from a distance may sometimes reflect a struggle between compassion and the realities that make compassionate action difficult.

This perspective shifts the conversation from a question of character to a question of conditions.

Rather than asking whether adolescents are compassionate, we might ask: What conditions help compassion become action?

The encouraging message from this research is that the factors influencing compassionate action are not fixed traits.

Relationships can be strengthened.

School climates can be improved.

Emotional regulation skills can be taught.

Prosocial values can be nurtured.

When we think about compassion this way, the goal becomes larger than helping young people recognize suffering. The goal is helping them develop the capacities that allow caring to become action.

Industry observers note that perhaps this is what adolescence reveals so clearly. The distance between caring and acting is rarely empty space. It is filled with questions about belonging, uncertainty, responsibility, and risk.

Young people are learning to navigate that space every day.

According to recent reports, our responsibility as the adults who support them is not simply to teach them to care. It is to create the relationships, communities, and opportunities that help them act on the care they already possess.

Tyralynn Frazier, Ph.D., MPH, is an associate research scientist at Emory University’s Center for Contemplative Science and Compassion-Based Ethics. She leads international research in partnership with local collaborators, examining how social, emotional, and ethical (SEE) Learning and CBCT for Educators are implemented, adapted, and sustained across cultural contexts.

#183392. Breaking: Scientists discover hidden brain changes linked to common sleep disorders

Breaking: Scientists discover hidden brain changes linked to common sleep disorders

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (937 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sleep disorders may have consequences that extend far beyond fatigue.
  • Published in the journal Scientific Reports, the research offers one of the broadest examinations yet of the brain changes associated with different sleep disorders.
  • What 57 Brain Imaging Studies Reveal About Sleep Disorders.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sleep disorders may have consequences that extend far beyond fatigue. Newly introduced research from Florida International University (FIU) has found that several types of sleep disorders are associated with physical changes in brain regions responsible for attention, motivation, and decision-making. These findings suggest that disrupted sleep may be connected to crucial differences in the brain's structure.

Published in the journal Scientific Reports, the research offers one of the broadest examinations yet of the brain changes associated with different sleep disorders. The discoveries could eventually help scientists identify sleep problems earlier and develop treatments tailored to the specific brain systems involved.

What 57 Brain Imaging Studies Reveal About Sleep Disorders.

An estimated 50 million to 70 million Americans experience sleep disorders, making them a major public health concern. To investigate their effects on the brain, scientists at FIU's Center for Children and Families combined and analyzed findings from 57 studies that used brain imaging to examine adults.

According to recent reports, rather than focusing on a single condition, the researchers compared several sleep disorders to determine whether they were associated with similar changes in brain structure. This approach, which is still relatively uncommon in sleep research, also allowed the team to identify differences specific to certain disorders.

Sources indicate that the analysis focused on two broad groups. The first, known as dyssomnias, includes insomnia and sleep apnea, conditions that interfere with falling asleep, staying asleep, or getting sufficient restorative sleep. The second group, called parasomnias, includes sleepwalking, nightmare disorder, and sleep terrors. These conditions involve unusual events or behaviors that interrupt normal sleep cycles.

Industry observers note that "As more people recognize how vital sleep is, there's growing urgency to understand what's happening in the brain," mentioned Matthew Sutherland, a cognitive neuroscientist at FIU and senior author of the study. "By bringing together results from many studies, this research gives us a clearer picture of how sleep disorders affect brain structure and function and where we need to focus next.".

Sleep Disorders Share Changes in a Critical Brain Region.

One of the most striking findings was that both groups of sleep disorders were associated with reductions in the thalamus, a structure deep within the brain that plays a central role in processing information, sustaining attention, and supporting complex thinking.

The researchers identified changes in a specific part of the thalamus called the pulvinar. This region helps the brain direct attention toward key information and manage cognitive control, which allows people to regulate their thoughts and actions while completing tasks.

The affected areas are connected to larger brain networks that help people concentrate, make decisions, and respond to their surroundings. Differences in these systems may help explain why people with sleep disorders often experience slower reaction times, difficulty making decisions, and a greater likelihood of errors or accidents.

"Most research looks at sleep disorders one at a time," stated Katharine Crooks, a recent FIU cognitive neuroscience doctoral graduate and lead author of the study. "By looking across many studies, we found shared patterns in the brain that help explain why sleep problems can impact focus, decision-making and everyday functioning. With so many people struggling with sleep, understanding what is happening in the brain is key to finding better interventions, diagnostic tools and personalized treatments.".

Sleepwalking and Nightmares Show Additional Brain Differences.

Although the researchers discovered common structural patterns across sleep disorders, they also found differences associated specifically with parasomnias.

People with these conditions revealed changes in the posterior cingulate cortex, a brain region involved in motivation, decision-making, and the regulation of emotions. This finding may help explain why disorders such as sleepwalking, recurring nightmares, and sleep terrors can sometimes be accompanied by difficulties with mood, behavior, or emotional control.

In contrast, the analysis did not reveal a consistent pattern of structural changes found exclusively in dyssomnias, the category that includes insomnia and sleep apnea.

Together, these results suggest that different forms of disrupted sleep may be associated with both shared and distinct changes in the brain. The particular regions involved may depend on the nature of the sleep disorder.

Could Brain Imaging Lead to Better Sleep Disorder Treatments?

The findings provide researchers with latest clues about the relationship between sleep disorders and the brain systems that support everyday thinking and behavior.

By identifying which regions are associated with particular sleep problems, scientists hope to improve diagnostic methods and develop more personalized interventions. Future treatments could potentially aim not only to improve sleep quality but also to protect the brain networks involved in attention, decision-making, and emotional regulation.

Sources indicate that however, an key question remains unanswered. The research identified associations between sleep disorders and differences in brain structure, but it did not establish whether disrupted sleep causes those differences, whether existing brain differences contribute to sleep disorders, or whether both processes occur.

To investigate this relationship further, the FIU team plans to examine individual parasomnias in greater detail, including sleepwalking and REM sleep behavior disorder.

Understanding how these conditions relate to changes in the brain could help researchers develop better ways to recognize, manage, and potentially prevent some of the cognitive and emotional difficulties associated with disrupted sleep.

Love Anyway

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You know that the price of life is death, that the price of love is loss, and still you watch the golden afternoon light fall on a face you love, knowing that the light will soon fade, knowing that the loving face too will one day fade to indifference or bone, and you love anyway — because life is transient but possible, because love alone bridges the impossible and the eternal.

I think about this and a passage from Louise Erdrich’s 2005 novel The Painted Drum (public library) flits across the sky of my mind:.

Life will break you. Nobody can protect you from that, and living alone won’t either, for solitude will also break you with its yearning. You have to love. You have to feel. It is the reason you are here on earth. You are here to risk your heart. You are here to be swallowed up. And when it happens that you are broken, or betrayed, or left, or hurt, or death brushes near, let yourself sit by an apple tree and listen to the apples falling all around you in heaps, wasting their sweetness. Tell yourself that you tasted as many as you could.

This, of course, is what life evolved to be — an aria of affirmation rising like luminous steam from the cold dark silence of an indifferent cosmos that will one day swallow all of it. Every living thing is its singer and its steward — something the poetic paleontologist Loren Eiseley captures with uncommon poignancy in his 1957 essay “The Judgment of the Birds,” found in his altogether magnificent posthumous collection The Star Thrower (public library).

Recent findings suggest that eiseley recounts resting beneath a tree after a day of trekking through fern and pine needles collecting fossils, dozing off in the warm sunlight, then being suddenly awakened by a great commotion to see “an enormous raven with a red and squirming nestling in his beak” perching on a crooked branch above. He writes:.

According to recent reports, into the glade fluttered small birds of half a dozen varieties drawn by the anguished outcries of the tiny parents. No one dared to attack the raven. But they cried there in some instinctive common misery, the bereaved and the unbereaved. The glade filled with their soft rustling and their cries. They fluttered as though to point their wings at the murderer. There was a dim intangible ethic he had violated, that they knew. He was a bird of death. And he, the murderer, the black bird at the heart of life, sat on there, glistening in the common light, formidable, unmoving, unperturbed, untouchable. The sighing died. It was then I saw the judgment. It was the judgment of life against death. I will never see it again so forcefully presented. I will never hear it again in notes so tragically prolonged. For in the midst of protest, they forgot the violence. There, in that clearing, the crystal note of a song sparrow lifted hesitantly in the hush. And finally, after painful fluttering, another took the song, and then another, the song passing from one bird to another, doubtfully at first, as though some evil thing were being slowly forgotten. Till suddenly they took heart and sang from many throats joyously together as birds are known to sing. They sang because life is sweet and sunlight beautiful. They sang under the brooding shadow of the raven. In simple truth they had forgotten the raven, for they were the singers of life, and not of death.

Couple with Hannah Arendt on love and how to live with the fundamental fear of loss, then revisit Loren Eiseley on the warblers and the wonder of being.

#183390. Tech Report: How Becoming a Parent Can Change Your Memories of Your Own Parents

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2218 w)

Tech Report: How Becoming a Parent Can Change Your Memories of Your Own Parents

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2218 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that it was around Christmas time when Emily* noticed that something was wrong.
  • It has been revealed that emily sought help from me in therapy just before Christmas when she realized that the prospect of spending the holidays with her parents was making it difficult for her to sleep and the few precious hours she had between feeds were taken up with anxious rumination.
  • Sources indicate that I work a lot with mothers and birthing people in the perinatal phase, and the change they experience in their relationship with their parents is something that comes up very frequently.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that it was around Christmas time when Emily* noticed that something was wrong. She had just welcomed her second son in September and still felt emotionally raw from the experience. Part of Emily’s postpartum planning had revolved around having her mum look after her three-year-old while she took care of the newly introduced baby. But every time she visited her parents, something in her tensed up, her mind went foggy, and instead of feeling the safety and relaxation she had been craving, she felt on edge.

It has been revealed that emily sought help from me in therapy just before Christmas when she realized that the prospect of spending the holidays with her parents was making it difficult for her to sleep and the few precious hours she had between feeds were taken up with anxious rumination. She couldn’t make any sense of it. It was like a switch had flipped and the previously supportive, albeit slightly emotionally disconnected, relationship she had had with her parents was in pieces.

Sources indicate that I work a lot with mothers and birthing people in the perinatal phase, and the change they experience in their relationship with their parents is something that comes up very frequently. Sometimes this change is positive, where they become more understanding of parents who were trying their best at the time. Sometimes it’s disorienting, like Emily’s, and the relationship seems to worsen. Either way, it’s vital to meet yourself with compassion and curiosity when unexpected feelings or memories resurface during this period of your life and try not to go through this transition on your own.

Emily came to see me for help with anxiety and insomnia, and a few sessions into our therapy she started to talk about memories that had been appearing for her, scenes from her childhood that suddenly had taken on newly introduced meaning or had popped up out of nowhere. It was as if her memories had changed, which made Emily feel crazy and even more anxious because she felt like she couldn’t trust herself anymore.

In the crudest terms, we tend to think of memory as a filing cabinet—a place where scenes, facts, annoying songs, and embarrassing moments are stored to be recalled, like when we try to remember what we had for dinner last week or where we went on holiday three years ago.

In a recent development, when I talk about memory with my clients, they usually understand that it is not a perfect system, that it can alter over time and be very subjective. What is harder to convey is that decades of research suggest that memory is not in fact a filing cabinet or a library catalogue—it’s a construction. Every time I try to remember where we went on holiday three summers ago, my brain doesn’t retrieve but rather constructs a memory of our trip to Italy. That means that each time we recall something, that memory can change slightly or take on new meaning. Researchers Daniel L. Schacter and Donna Rose Addis found that, in fact, remembering and imagining look very similar in terms of activation in the brain.

Why does that matter? It can help make sense of what happened to Emily and what happens to many of my clients when they become parents and their relationships with their own parents change. Some of this is explained by a shift in roles: When a child becomes a parent, the dynamic of the child-parent relationship naturally has to change, which can be difficult for both parties. Grandparents and newly introduced parents might find it challenging to adapt to who is in charge and “who knows best.” But sometimes the difficulty is more subtle, and it’s related to memory.

Emily struggled because she had started to have visceral memories of herself at about three to five years old, even though she had never actively thought about her childhood much before. She associated that phase in her life with a feeling of paralysis that she couldn’t explain. She told me how exhausted she felt every time she left her parents’ house now, like she had been holding her breath for hours.

Emily knew from whispered family stories that her mother had dealt with bouts of depression through much of her childhood. She also knew that her parents’ marriage hadn’t always been as placid and quiet as it was now. She had always had memories of them fighting late at night but had never thought much of it. Now she remembered her mother in tears, shouting and doors slamming. She remembered hiding under her bed.

Memory is heavily influenced by our current state of mind. Martin Conway, in his papers on autobiographical memory, explains that when we try to retrieve a memory or remember something spontaneously, we construct that memory in the moment, partly based on our current goals. If we are hungry, we might construct a memory of a cafe we saw on our walk two weeks ago. If we have a fight with our partner, we might suddenly remember all the times they disappointed us, when we usually are able to accept their imperfections.

When Emily became a parent, her goals changed dramatically, and it changed what memories her brain predicted might be useful for her.

Articles that explore holiday stress management, managing conflict, picking gifts, making resolutions, and more.

Emily realized that her experience of being her son’s age was one of bracing and zoning out because she had felt disconnected from her mother and scared of her father at the time. As a parent, Emily was suddenly able to attune to what it felt like for her to be three years old. Her three-year-old self did not feel safe, and she did not believe her child was safe, either.

Sources indicate that conway notes that the memories we are able to construct have to be coherent with how we think of ourselves, our beliefs about ourselves, and the world and people in it. According to Conway’s theory, our brains filter, rationalize, or dismiss memories that are inconsistent with who we believe we are.

Sources indicate that before Emily had children, she believed, largely unconsciously, that her childhood experiences were irrelevant to who she was and that she hadn’t really been affected by them. When she became a mum, her visceral memories of childhood fear did not match up with who she believed she was anymore. Her goals had changed from surviving and rationalizing to tuning in to and protecting her child. Her brain was telling her she had to shield her child from something that she had experienced as frightening as a child.

Other clients of mine have found that becoming a parent had the opposite effect. They were able to look at the younger versions of their parents with more compassion and kindness, reconstructing memories through the eyes of an exhausted parent who was trying and barely coping.

Karen and her parents had had a difficult relationship. Karen’s parents divorced when she was young, and Karen had always felt her mother had been unavailable when she was a child. She experienced a lot of anger when thinking about her childhood. She had memories of having to take on responsibilities too early, looking after her siblings, and cooking and cleaning while her mother was at work. Karen had purposefully moved away from her parents and had spent years asserting her independence. She had never wanted children because she had such strong memories of what it had been like to be a young caretaker and not being able to feel like a child. When she met her husband, she realized that creating her own family was more vital to her than she had thought.

Karen came to see me for anxiety. She was worried about losing her freedom when she became a mother, and we thought about how her childhood experiences shaped her experience now. I saw Karen for quite some time after she gave birth, and something shifted for her when she became a parent. She remembered instances of seeing her mother frazzled, rushed, and overwhelmed and how hard she had tried to find time to be there for Karen and her siblings. Karen started to realize how impossible it must have been for her mother to raise three children on her own while working.

Sources indicate that karen tried to talk to her mother and learned about how ashamed she was for burdening her daughter and unsure about whether Karen wanted her in her life. To her surprise, Karen experienced her mother’s relationship with her own daughter as reparative. She could make sense of her anger and her need for freedom and see that what happened in her childhood was not something her mother had intended.

Sources indicate that for Emily, too, her experiences meant she had to rebuild the relationship with her mother and find a more honest foundation. She was able to have conversations with her about what it would have been like for Emily growing up, and, to Emily’s surprise, her mother also listened and apologized for not having checked in with her sooner. It started a healing process for Emily that involved listening to what her three-year-old self might have felt and acknowledging that she had been trying to rationalize her way out of feeling for most of her life. She had to slowly let herself experience that her parents were safe now; she decided to not rely on them for child care but let the relationship grow more slowly.

According to recent reports, what helped Emily was hearing her mother validate what happened to her as a child. It was something Emily would have needed when she was younger. She was also able to make new meaning of her relationship with her parents through therapy—an act of shared social construction with another human, the therapist, that fulfills some of our core needs of being heard, seen, and understood.

Industry observers note that karen similarly needed to feel heard by her mother. Her anger dissipated when she was able to put herself into her mother’s shoes and see that her and her mother’s experience could exist side by side.

What can you do if parenthood is shifting your relationship with your own parents? Here are steps that I have found are helpful for my clients.

Find support. The first step in coping with a difficult experience is to not try to go through it alone. We are social beings who need to feel understood by others. Seek out a friend or a sibling if you are struggling with feelings you do not understand.

According to recent reports, meet yourself with self-compassion. When strong emotions come up, we might tell ourselves, “I’m overreacting,” “I’m too sensitive,” “I just need to get on with things and stop complaining.” Self-criticism can perpetuate a cycle in which we invalidate our experiences until they become impossible to ignore. It also won’t help to be overly critical of yourself if you believe you’ve been judging your parents too harshly, now that you have the perspective of being a parent yourself.

Recent findings suggest that seek out conversations. If thinking back on your childhood memories brings up a perspective change on your childhood, speak to your family, your parents or siblings, and learn about how they experienced that time and you as a child. It might help you feel more compassion with your parents who may have been struggling, and can also help you understand yourself better as a person.

Recent findings suggest that set boundaries, if needed. If memories from your childhood suddenly take on new meaning, it might be important to think about boundaries and clear rules to set with your child’s grandparents. If you felt unsafe or uncomfortable as a child, it is OK to make it clear how you expect the adults in your child’s life to behave. This can, of course, be easier said than done, and it can be useful to seek help to deal with feelings of guilt or anxiety around setting boundaries with your parents.

Seek out professional help. Remember that every experience is subjective—your version of what happened might be different from that of your siblings or your parents. That does not make it any less valid. While Emily was lucky that her mother acknowledged her experience, your family members might not always be so receptive and might be more defensive about any wrongdoing. Seeking professional help can be especially useful when you are dealing with a family system that is less likely to take responsibility or want to change.

Becoming a parent changes your world in a thousand ways and can dramatically alter the way you look at your own childhood. Self-compassion is hugely key in navigating all the transformations you might go through as a new parent. Finding others that meet you with understanding and care is the first step in making sure you can meet yourself and your child in the same way.

*The stories in this article are a combination of experiences of several clients; any identifying information has been changed.

Sarah Emmerson, PsychD, is a chartered counseling psychologist and cofounder of Talking Women, a private psychology practice in London specializing in women's mental health.

Breaking: Six Factors That Support Mental Health for Black Youth

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1311 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, on a summer day at UC Berkeley, four teenagers jostled at a whiteboard, vying to write down their solutions to an important public health concern.
  • Recent findings suggest that in the United States, deaths by suicide have been surging among Black kids and teens for decades.
  • As the teenagers brainstormed, Jasmin Brooks Stephens, a Berkeley assistant professor of psychology, watched nearby.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, on a summer day at UC Berkeley, four teenagers jostled at a whiteboard, vying to write down their solutions to an important public health concern. They were having fun even as they took on a heavy task: helping researchers design programs to reduce the skyrocketing suicide rate among Black youth.

Recent findings suggest that in the United States, deaths by suicide have been surging among Black kids and teens for decades. For those between 10 and 17 years of age, the suicide rate rose 144% from 2007 to 2020. What’s more, Black boys die by suicide more than twice as frequently as Black girls, although the suicide rate for Black girls increased by 182% between 2001 and 2017.

As the teenagers brainstormed, Jasmin Brooks Stephens, a Berkeley assistant professor of psychology, watched nearby. The moment was a highlight in research she was conducting with the Homeless Children’s Network on improving mental health outcomes for Black youth. Brooks Stephens believed that teens themselves have meaningful ideas to share, and she had worked for eight weeks with these particular teenagers, who were part of the network’s Jabali Youth Advocacy organization, culminating in their trip to campus.

Sources indicate that “One of the most exciting things was seeing them all jump up and say, ‘Wait, we can make a program for making us feel better? We have the power to do that?’” Brooks Stephens recalled. “Seeing them find and discover that sense of agency in themselves—that was invaluable to me.” It also was one of the few times any of the teens had visited a college campus, she mentioned, an added bonus. In future work, Brooks Stephens prepares to translate the results of her study for clinicians and policymakers who are trying to improve suicide prevention for Black youth.

In a recent development, the ongoing project is just one example of how Brooks Stephens is working to address rising suicide rates among Black youth by engaging them in participatory research—an unusual and hopeful approach in suicide prevention studies. “This summer I had the incredible opportunity to work alongside young people to design a program that would help other young people want to live,” she said. “Rather than waiting until a young person is already in crisis, I’m interested in understanding what helps youth thrive—what gives them hope and a sense of possibility and helps them recognize the brilliance they have inside them.”.

Despite the growing crisis among Black youth, suicide rates are dropping for adolescents in the U.S. overall. Brooks Stephens finds these statistics revealing: “To me, that suggests that the approaches we have relied on have not adequately addressed the conditions driving suicide risk in Black communities,” she said.

Industry observers note that it’s easy to talk about structural racism as an abstract concept, or personal encounters with racists as disturbing but bounded moments. But grappling with racism heavily impacts Black youth and increases their suicide risk, according to a 2023 report from the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. Indeed, Brooks Stephens has published work documenting how racial discrimination and the COVID-19 pandemic, which disproportionately harmed Black Americans, together worsened suicide risk for Black young adults.

Brooks Stephens’s work is informed by both her research and her own experience of how race can shape young people’s sense of self. “I became aware very early on that Black children are often navigating expectations about who they are supposed to be before they have even had the opportunity to figure out who they are for themselves,” she said. “That has stayed with me—the importance of creating space for Black young people to define themselves, recognize their strengths, and imagine who they want to become.” At the same time, she saw how the stigma surrounding mental health could make it harder for Black youth and families to seek support, even as racism and other chronic stressors were impacting their well-being.

In a recent development, when she took an African American psychology class as an undergraduate at the University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, with Enrique Neblett, a renowned scholar of race and health who became her mentor, Brooks Stephens saw the connection between those experiences—and found her passion. “I realized that there was an entire field devoted to understanding how racism affects mental health and how Black children come to understand themselves and their racial identity,” she said.

Later, during her doctoral research at the University of Houston, Brooks Stephens worked with Rheeda Walker, an expert on suicide science and African American adult mental health research. Brooks Stephens noticed that there was very limited discussion about building upstream resilience in suicide prevention research—an approach that focuses on child well-being and happiness before the development of a mental health crisis.

Sources indicate that “We’re studying why people choose to end their life without understanding what makes people want to live,” she mentioned. For Brooks Stephens, that realization opened up a different way of thinking about suicide prevention, one that made room for the strengths that were often absent from traditional models, such as racial identity, spirituality, family connection, belonging, or hope.

It has been revealed that brooks Stephens knows she can’t single-handedly eliminate the racial traumas faced by young Black people. Nor can she end other factors that lead to higher suicide rates in her community, such as systemic injustice or poverty. Instead, she’s focusing on where she can make a difference through her research.

“While I may not be able to eradicate racism, I can help build programs that change how Black young people see themselves and their futures—programs that help them feel grounded in their identity and able to imagine a life that feels worth living,” she said.

Brooks Stephens and her colleagues identified six positive factors that reduce suicidality among Black youth (courtesy of Jasmin Brooks Stephens).

As a first step, this year she and her colleagues created the Black Youth Thriving Framework for Suicide Prevention. It’s based on a literature review that identified six protective factors that can reduce suicidality among Black youth, including family support, community ties, and self-acceptance. “What we’re working to identify now are the strategies that can help cultivate those strengths in young people’s lives,” Brooks Stephens mentioned.

Already, in a study from 2023, she and her colleagues indicated that Black young adults with stronger feelings of self-acceptance are less vulnerable to depression and suicide. Likewise, she has identified mindfulness and meditation as potential tools for Black Americans in their early 20s to buffer the impulsivity that is often associated with suicide risk.

This approach is a radical departure from the status quo. Right now, resources for preventing suicide orbit around moments of crisis, Brooks Stephens stated. When a child shows signs of depression or arrives at a hospital following a suicide attempt, that’s when an intervention is often provided. Brooks Stephens wants to develop research-backed ways to prevent a child from ever getting to that troubling point in the first place.

And, increasingly, she is asking Black young people themselves to help determine what those approaches should look like. Brooks Stephens remarked that the four teens with whom she worked this summer were not simply research participants; they were collaborators in imagining what suicide prevention could become.

“It’s very uplifting for me because I’m bringing underserved voices into our research and I’m designing solutions,” she said. “And those solutions are how we make kids want to live and love themselves. That’s it. It’s loving themselves, loving their life. That’s what I’m helping them discover.”.

#183388. Magic mushrooms rewire the brain in a way scientists didn't expect
